adhd-cope.text: if you can’t start, lower the cost of starting. open the doc. leave the cursor blinking. that counts.
two-minute rule: if it takes less than 2 minutes, do it now. don’t add it to the list.
when the brain says ‘i’ll do it later,’ replace ‘later’ with a specific time. or it doesn’t exist.
body doubling works. sit near someone working. it doesn’t matter what they’re doing.
transitions are the hardest part of any task. budget time for the gap between two things.
if the room is too loud, the task is twice as hard. close one tab. close one door. close one window.
write the next action, not the project. ‘open laptop’ is doable. ‘finish the report’ is not.
set a timer for 5 minutes. you can stop after. you usually won’t, but you can.
the dishes don’t get done by thinking about the dishes. start the water.
put your phone in another room. the friction of walking is enough.
one tab. one document. one task. close everything else.
if you forgot what you were doing, that’s information. write down what you remember.
the brain is not bad at planning. it’s bad at predicting how it will feel later. plan for tired-you.
lay clothes out the night before. that’s not childish. that’s saving you a decision.
waiting is the killer. while the kettle boils, do one thing. one.
medication helps the door open. it doesn’t walk through it for you.
mid-afternoon crash is biology, not failure. eat something. lie down for ten.
if the task has more than three steps, break it. write the steps. cross them off as you go.
caffeine works until it doesn’t. notice when you’ve passed the peak.
hyperfocus burns fuel fast. set an alarm. drink water. stand up.
if you’ve been meaning to do it for a week, it’s not the task. it’s the activation cost. lower it.
don’t open the email app. open the one email you need. type the reply. close.
paper lists work better than apps when the brain is loud.
a half-done task is not a failed task. it’s a task with a bookmark.
external structure is not a crutch. it’s the right tool for a brain that runs different software.
the deadline is not the start time. the start time is days before. mark it on the calendar.
the brain rewards novelty. add novelty to the boring task — different room, different drink, different chair.
if you can’t focus, walk. ten minutes. the brain reorders itself when the body moves.
write the task on a sticky note. put it on the laptop. that’s the system.
the urge to start every task is the wrong target. the urge to finish one task is rarer. protect it.
a meeting that could be an email is real. but a task that could be five minutes is also real. start the five.
don’t multitask between two cognitive tasks. you’re switching, not doing both.
the working-memory list is full. write things down even if it feels excessive.
if you’ve been in the same chair for three hours and the task isn’t moving, the chair is the problem. move.
notice what time of day you actually focus. protect that window.
the laundry, the dishes, the email — none of it is moral. it’s just stuff that needs doing.
start the task badly. you can fix it once it exists. you can’t fix what you haven’t started.
if the prompt is too vague, write a smaller one. ‘draft email to landlord’ is a task. ‘deal with apartment’ is not.
you don’t have to feel motivated. you have to put your hands on the keyboard.
the adhd tax — late fees, replacement charges, missed deadlines — is the cost of a brain not built for paperwork.
when stuck, narrate out loud what you’re doing. it splits the task into smaller voiced steps.
the snowball method works because finishing the small thing tells the brain it can finish things.
if you’re avoiding a task, ask: what’s the smallest version of this i could do in 60 seconds.
the right tool isn’t the perfect tool. it’s the one you’ll actually open.
don’t set up the system today. use the system tomorrow. setup is procrastination in disguise.
you’re allowed to have one boring system that works, even if it’s not pretty.
a forgotten thing is not proof you don’t care. it’s proof a ball dropped that other brains catch automatically.
if it’s in your head, it’s not on the list. write it on the list.
the energy crash after a good day is real. plan for it. the next day is allowed to be small.
starting late doesn’t mean starting badly. it means starting later than you planned. those aren’t the same.

anxiety-ground.text: feel the chair under you. feel where your back ends and the chair begins.
name the room you’re in. name what’s behind you. name what’s in front of you. that’s enough.
your hands. press them together. notice the warmth. that warmth is yours.
five things you can see. four you can touch. three you can hear. two you can smell. one you can taste.
press both feet flat on the floor. notice you’re held.
the breath is here. you don’t have to make it deeper. you just have to find it.
cold water on the wrists. cold water on the back of the neck. the body resets faster than the mind.
count backward from twenty. slowly. by the time you get to zero, the room is still here.
find one object in the room. describe it to yourself in detail — color, edge, weight.
your jaw is probably tight. let it loosen. let the tongue rest against the roof of the mouth.
put one hand on the chest and one on the belly. see which one moves first.
inhale for four. hold for four. exhale for six. the longer exhale tells the body it’s safe.
notice the texture under your fingers. fabric, wood, glass, paper. notice it without naming.
the panic is a wave. waves crest. they don’t stay at the top forever.
the floor is here. the wall is here. the ceiling is here. the room has not moved.
press your palms against a wall. notice your weight push back into the body.
you don’t have to fix the thought. you have to let the body know it’s not under attack.
your shoulders are probably up near your ears. let them drop. that one move is enough.
ice cubes in the hands. hold for thirty seconds. the cold gives the brain something else to work on.
find the longest exhale you can make. don’t force the inhale. just let air leave.
you’re allowed to lie on the floor. the floor is solid. it has been solid the whole time.
notice which parts of the body you can feel right now. notice which are quiet. that’s a map.
the heart racing is doing its job. it’s not broken. it’s just loud.
wrap your arms around yourself. press into the shoulders. that’s a hold. it counts.
the thought that something is wrong is not the same as something being wrong.
if you can hear your breath, you’re breathing. if you’re breathing, you have time.
one foot. then the other. notice the weight shift. you can walk if you need to.
name three colors you can see. just colors. nothing more.
the body is older than the panic. the body has been here longer than this thought.
push against something solid — a doorframe, a counter, a wall. let the body remember it’s strong.
drink water. cold if possible. swallow. notice the swallow.
you don’t have to slow your breath. you have to notice it’s still happening.
look out the window. find one thing far away. let the eyes rest on distance.
count your fingers. ten. count them again. that’s a thing the body can do that the mind can’t argue with.
lower the lights. quiet rooms hold panicking nervous systems better than bright ones.
you can take up the whole couch. spread the limbs. let the body be big.
press the tongue against the roof of the mouth. hold. release. simple, cheap, works.
there is no test here. you don’t have to do this right.
notice the sound farthest from you. then the sound closest. you have hearing. it is working.
wash your hands slowly. warm water. notice the temperature. notice the soap.
if standing is hard, sit. if sitting is hard, lie down. the body knows which to choose.
find one thing in the room that hasn’t changed since yesterday. that’s an anchor.
the panic wants to leave. you don’t have to chase it out. let it find the door.
hum. just a low hum. the vagus nerve responds to vibration in the throat.
if you can name what you’re feeling, the feeling has already lost some of its weight.
cold air on the face. step outside if you can. the temperature change is information for the body.
one slow blink. then another. the body uses these to mark time.
you don’t have to remember the technique. you have to notice you’re already breathing.
anchor your eyes on one corner of the room. don’t track. just rest there.
the ground holds you whether you trust it or not. that’s the deal.

cbt-microlesson.text: the thought that says ‘always’ is rarely a fact. it’s a feeling pretending to be a fact.
if you wouldn’t say it to a friend, the thought is using the wrong voice.
predicting the future feels like a fact. it isn’t.
the worst-case scenario your brain just wrote is one possible scenario, not the only one.
‘i feel stupid’ is a feeling. ‘i am stupid’ is a story the feeling told.
one bad day is one bad day. it isn’t proof of a pattern.
when the brain says ‘everyone thinks this,’ check who ‘everyone’ actually is.
mind reading is a skill no one has. that thing you assume they think — you don’t actually know.
‘should’ is a word that lives in someone else’s voice. notice whose.
if the only options the brain offers are perfect or failed, the brain is leaving out a lot.
taking blame for something that happened to you is a strategy your brain learned. it isn’t accuracy.
one piece of evidence isn’t a verdict. it’s one piece of evidence.
the thought ‘i’ll never get over this’ is a feeling about now, not a forecast.
labeling yourself with one word — ‘lazy,’ ‘broken,’ ‘failure’ — collapses everything you are into one syllable.
the sentence ‘i ruined it’ often means ‘something hard happened.’ those are different sentences.
the brain is not a journalist. it’s an editorialist with a deadline.
catastrophe-thinking solves no future catastrophe. it just costs the present moment.
notice when you say ‘i’m bad at this’ after one attempt. once isn’t a sample size.
the feeling that something terrible is about to happen is a feeling. it has been wrong before.
when the thought arrives in the second person — ‘you idiot’ — that’s a voice. it isn’t yours.
taking credit for the bad and not the good is a pattern, not the truth.
‘they didn’t text back because they hate me’ has a hundred other endings.
if the thought rhymes or sounds catchy, treat it like a slogan. slogans aren’t analysis.
the brain can be very confident and very wrong at the same time.
discomfort is not danger. they share a hallway but they aren’t the same room.
the thought ‘i can’t handle this’ is what the brain says before it handles things.
one missed deadline isn’t proof you can’t do deadlines. it’s proof one deadline got missed.
‘i feel like a failure, therefore i am a failure.’ the comma does not connect those.
the past predicts patterns, not destinies.
if every option in your head is bad, ask: is there an option not in my head yet.
‘i feel guilty’ is sometimes information. sometimes it’s static. you can ask which.
when the thought speeds up, the truth is usually still going at normal speed.
you don’t have to argue with the thought. you have to notice it’s a thought.
the urge to apologize for being upset is the same pattern that made you upset. notice it. don’t follow it.
‘no one cares’ is what the brain says when one person didn’t.
if the thought begins with ‘always’ or ‘never,’ add ‘right now’ and see if it still holds.
the conclusion ‘i’m a burden’ is usually older than the situation that triggered it.
comparing your inside to someone else’s outside is comparing a kitchen to a magazine cover.
the brain offers thoughts. you don’t have to accept every delivery.
saying ‘i’m overreacting’ is sometimes the thing that stops you from listening to a real signal.
the thought ‘this will last forever’ has been saying that for years. it has been wrong every time.
you can feel something is true and have it not be true.
when the brain offers two options — both bad — there are usually three.
the harshest voice in your head is rarely the most informed one.
‘they’re better than me’ is a sentence with no measurement attached.
the worst thing you said to yourself today, you wouldn’t say to anyone else. notice the asymmetry.
one small thing going wrong is not a long chain of dominoes. that’s the brain rendering a movie.
‘i ruined the day’ is a much smaller event than the day. usually a day has hours that weren’t ruined.
if you’re trying to figure out who’s at fault, you might be in the wrong question.
the thought ‘i should be over this by now’ has no clock attached. there is no clock for this.

therapeutic-quote.text: you are the sky. everything else is just the weather.
nothing ever goes away until it has taught us what we need to know.
start where you are.
feel the feelings and drop the story.
things falling apart is a kind of testing and a kind of healing.
fear is a natural reaction to moving closer to the truth.
compassion is a relationship between equals.
the present moment is the only moment available to us.
no mud, no lotus.
letting go gives us freedom.
feelings come and go like clouds in a windy sky.
to be beautiful means to be yourself.
smile, breathe, and go slowly.
what we don’t need in the midst of struggle is shame for being human.
shame derives its power from being unspeakable.
feelings are not facts.
imperfection is a natural part of existing.
you do not have to be good.
attention is the beginning of devotion.
pay attention. be astonished. tell about it.
let everything happen to you. no feeling is final.
be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart.
the cure for pain is in the pain.
the wound is the place where the light enters you.
this being human is a guest house.
i can be changed by what happens to me. but i refuse to be reduced by it.
there is no greater agony than bearing an untold story inside you.
we may encounter many defeats but we must not be defeated.
when i accept myself just as i am, then i can change.
what i am is good enough if i would only be it openly.
the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are.
there is no coming to consciousness without pain.
we cannot change anything until we accept it.
between stimulus and response there is a space.
when we cannot change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.
almost everything will work again if you unplug it for a few minutes.
expectations are resentments under construction.
you own everything that happened to you.
the antidote to exhaustion is not rest, but wholeheartedness.
anything that does not bring you alive is too small for you.
caring for myself is not self-indulgence, it is self-preservation.
we’re all just walking each other home.
when i let go of what i am, i become what i might be.
your pain is the breaking of the shell that encloses your understanding.
the risk to remain tight in a bud became more painful than the risk to blossom.
the most basic way to connect with another person is to listen.
the most important thing we ever give each other is our attention.
i wish i could show you the astonishing light of your own being.
the path out of hell is through misery.
radical acceptance is not approval. it is acknowledgment of what is.

quote-permission.text: you have power over your mind, not outside events. find your strength there.
the impediment to action advances action. what stands in the way becomes the way.
waste no more time arguing what a good person should be. be one.
the happiness of your life depends on the quality of your thoughts.
you could leave life right now. let that determine what you do and say.
we suffer more in imagination than in reality.
it is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.
the whole future lies in uncertainty: live immediately.
difficulties strengthen the mind, as labor does the body.
no person is free who is not master of themselves.
it’s not what happens to you, but how you react to it that matters.
first say to yourself what you would be; then do what you have to do.
make the best use of what is in your power, and take the rest as it happens.
circumstances don’t make the person, they reveal them to themselves.
you will never know who you are unless you push past your perceived limits.
the most important conversations you’ll ever have are the ones with yourself.
the only real test of intelligence is if you get what you want out of life.
a calm mind, a fit body, a house full of love. these can’t be bought.
happiness is a choice you make and a skill you develop.
you do not rise to the level of your goals; you fall to the level of your systems.
every action you take is a vote for the type of person you wish to become.
habits are the compound interest of self-improvement.
clarity about what matters provides clarity about what does not.
human beings are at their best when immersed deeply in something challenging.
compare yourself to who you were yesterday, not to who someone else is today.
set your house in perfect order before you criticize the world.
nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it.
we can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness.
everything can be taken from a man but one thing: to choose one’s attitude.
when we can no longer change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.
between stimulus and response there is a space — in it lies our freedom to choose.
quote-permission.note: widely attributed to viktor frankl; not found in his writings (popularized by stephen covey).

quote-permission.text: you have to build a life worth living.
act opposite to the emotion’s urge, all the way, and the feeling will shift.
quote-permission.note: after marsha linehan’s dbt opposite-action skill.

quote-permission.text: nothing ever goes away until it has taught us what we need to know.
we can let the circumstances of our lives harden us, or soften us.
feeling compassion for ourselves in no way releases us from responsibility.
the boundary to what we can accept is the boundary to our freedom.
the curious paradox is that when i accept myself as i am, then i can change.
what is most personal is most universal.
with self-compassion, we give ourselves the kindness we’d give a good friend.
the wound is the place where the light enters you.
you are not a drop in the ocean. you are the ocean in a drop.
instructions for living a life: pay attention. be astonished. tell about it.
tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?
let everything happen to you: beauty and terror. just keep going.
be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart.
the antidote to exhaustion is not rest. it is wholeheartedness.
start close in, don’t take the second step. start with the first thing.
action isn’t the product of motivation. motivation is the product of action.
quote-permission.note: behavioral-activation adage; widely repeated, no single source.

quote-permission.text: make the habit tiny, then celebrate it. the feeling is what makes it stick.
emotions create habits — not repetition, not frequency.
discipline is choosing between what you want now and what you want most.
quote-permission.note: commonly misattributed to abraham lincoln; origin unknown.

quote-permission.text: you don’t have to see the whole staircase, just take the first step.
the secret of getting ahead is getting started.
quote-permission.note: commonly attributed to mark twain; unverified.

quote-permission.text: done is better than perfect.
quote-permission.note: popularized by sheryl sandberg as a facebook engineering motto.

quote-permission.text: a year from now, you may wish you had started today.
your brain isn’t broken. it runs on interest, urgency, novelty, and challenge.
quote-permission.note: after william dodson’s interest-based nervous system model of adhd.

quote-permission.text: lower the bar until you can step over it. then step over it.
start before you feel ready. the readiness comes from starting.
the task you’re dreading is rarely as big as the dread around it.
